en: Preface to the *Brief Account of Eminent Monks of West Lake in Wulin*:

Human life in this world of five turbidities is steeped in the defilements of the sense bases and objects; mired in confusion and sinking into ignorance, those who are able to escape this burning house are but few.
To shave one’s head, don the black robes, and become a monk is already to stand far above the common crowd. However...
For a monk to be a true monk, how could he stop at this alone? He must realize the mind and see the nature to transcend birth and death;
he must maintain the precepts with purity through long and diligent accumulation; and he must expound the teachings to establish a model for the future.

Among hundreds of thousands or millions of monks, such individuals appear but once or twice—distinguished, magnificent, and so preeminent that they cannot be matched. Among all the followers of the Buddha in the world, there are none who do not revere them.
One looks up to them; this is why there are biographies of eminent monks. There have been those who composed them, those who read them, and again, those who practiced according to them.

Yet, none have yet gone so far as to contemplate these men, follow in their footsteps, and, imagining their lofty character, erect magnificent pavilions at the very sites where they formerly walked or sat in meditation to honor and revere them, recording their deeds and conduct.
He praised it with verses. As for the one who depicted the *uṣṇīṣa* and looked upon it with reverence, it was the Maṇi lecturer Yuanjing Jie’an who accomplished this.
The pavilion was first founded by the former abbot Liaoxing; before the work was completed, he moved to another monastery.
Jie’an truly succeeded him in completing it. He first gathered renowned masters who had previously resided at Qiantang.
Twenty-four individuals were thus identified. I commissioned the monk Yuanfu of Dongjia to verify the facts and compose eulogies for them.

Subsequently, through further searches, six more individuals were found; Jie’an compiled their accounts and composed eulogies for them as well. Their portraits were painted and enshrined in a pavilion.
Fearing that these might not circulate throughout the four quarters, I combined them into a single volume titled *Xihu Gao*.

The *Sengshi lüe* (A Brief History of the Sangha) has been carved into woodblocks to benefit students. Alas! The Buddha-dharma flourished in the southeast, and extraordinary individuals emerged in succession.

Those who came before have already been held in high esteem by those who followed; as the lamp is passed from one to another to continue the life-force of the Buddha’s wisdom, it is my deep hope that future generations will, in turn, hold their successors in even higher regard.
Preface by Mo Ziwen of Wu Commandery on the Day of the Winter Solstice in the Bingchen Year of Baoyou.

The Master’s name was Huiri. He was a man from Western India who came to this land at the beginning of the Xianhe era of the Eastern Jin dynasty.
Upon arriving in Hangzhou, he saw that the mountain crags were exquisite and beautiful, and said: "This is but a small portion of Vulture Peak in my home country of Central India.
I know not in what year it flew here. When the Buddha was in the world, it was mostly hidden by immortals and spirits; is it not the same here now? [He entered] the cave.

Originally, there were two monkeys, one black and one white. He called to them, and they emerged at his voice. People began to believe him, and from this, Flying Eagle Peak (Feilaidong) derived its name.
The Master then established two monasteries on the site: first Lingjiu and later Lingyin.
He frequently sat in meditation within a rock cave, which consequently became known as Layman Li’s Cave (Ligongyan). His burial stupa remains there to this day. The eulogy says:
A solitary peak flies forth, from west to east; the Master also arrives there and points out its traces.
The Cave of the Calling Monkeys is cold; he sits in meditative repose within the empty crag. Flowers bloom and fall; how many times has the spring breeze passed?
—By Chao Fa-shi of Qi Yuquan.
The Master’s name was Tanchao; his surname was Zhang, and he was a native of Qinghe. He stood eight chi tall, maintained a vegetarian diet, and wore simple cloth garments.

He dwelt alone in the mountain forests, where even tigers and rhinoceroses did not harm him. Toward the end of the Jianyuan era, he took up residence at Lingyuan Mountain in Qiantang, where he regularly lectured on the sutras during the summer months.
An old man came to listen to the teachings. When [the Master] questioned him regarding his surname and clan, he replied, "I am not a human;
I am a dragon. I dwell at the foot of Deer Mountain (Lùshān) in Fùchūn. The local villagers have excavated the mountain, encroaching upon my abode.

In anger, I have withheld rain for many months now. I beg you, Master, to go once and instruct the dragons. The Master granted his request and said, "In this place of mine as well, there is no water. You..."
"Can you bring this about? The old man then clapped his hands, and the spring gushed forth spontaneously; it is the Jade Spring (Yùquán) that exists today.

The Master then went there to establish an altar and administer the precepts to the dragon. While he lectured on the sutras from a floating boat, the rain fell in great abundance, thoroughly moistening the earth. This occurred in the third year of the Jiading era.
He was bestowed the title of Great Master Lingwu (Numinous Enlightenment).
The eulogy says: Body and world both forgotten, he triumphed through the Way. In the Garden of the Spirit he expounded the sutras, and dragons came to listen.
When he sought water, springs arose; when he prayed for rain, it fell in response. What did the dragon do? It was simply the Master’s command.

The Master Guanzhi of Lower Zhu during the Sui dynasty was named Zhen Guan, with the courtesy name Shengda. He was of the Fan clan of Qiantang; his family had long been distinguished officials. From birth, the Master possessed extraordinary physical characteristics.
His tongue had purple veins; the palms of both his hands bore the marks of the *ṛṣi* (sage) script. Having left the household life, he mastered the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.

At that time, Yan remarked, "In Qiantang there is Zhen Guan; the Buddha-dharma shall occupy half the world. He subsequently visited Zhiyi of Tiantai and requested instruction in dhyāna and contemplation.
Because Zhiyi was of the same age as his teacher, he treated him merely as a brother in the Dharma. In the fifteenth year of the Kaihuang era, at...
The dhūta practitioner resided in a stone chamber on the peak of Lingyin Mountain. The assembly built the Nantianzhu Temple to the south and invited the Master to dwell there;
he thus became the founding patriarch of that monastery. He constantly lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra*, regarding it as his essential practice.

Moved by the spirit of Gaotingshan’s request for a lecture, the spirit relinquished its shrine to serve as a Buddha hall. Whenever the Master washed his hands, the remaining droplets did not moisten the ground—a phenomenon that people found particularly extraordinary.
The Master possessed refined integrity. Emperor Wen summoned him three times, and the Prince of Qin invited him twice; on both occasions, he declined on the grounds of illness.
During the Daye era, while traveling through the mountains, he personally marked out the site for his burial. Not long after, he manifested the signs of passing away.

He dreamed that he was returning to the mountain with Zhiyi and his peers, escorting the Buddha. Upon waking, he sighed and said: "I was destined to end my life at sixty-two, but through the power of lecturing on the *Lotus Sūtra*, I extended it by twelve years. Now..."
Seventy-four. His life’s span having come to an end, he entered nirvana at midnight. His stupa was located on East Ridge; it had long been abandoned and left unrepaired.
During the Tianxi era, Ciyun reconstructed it. The eulogy says:
The wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle was expounded by the Patriarch of the Tiantai School; His years matched [the Buddha’s] and his Way was the same—truly worthy of following in his footsteps.
Though summons from the imperial court were frequent, he did not move from his steadfast pillar; His pure wind is chillingly majestic, capable of stirring the ages for a thousand autumns.
—The Monk of a Thousand Years from Central India.
The Master’s name was Baozhang (Jewel-Palms). He was a native of Central India who traveled east during the Wei and Jin dynasties.

He claimed to be six hundred and seventy-three years old and stated that he was born in the *dingmao* year, the twelfth year of King Weilie of the Zhou dynasty. His left hand was always clenched in a fist, and a pearl was visible within his palm.
He took this as his name. He first traveled to Mount Wǔtái and Mount Éméi, then returned south to Mount Héng and Mount Lú.

Entering Jiānyè, he met Bodhidharma at the Liáng court and subsequently inquired into the Dharma. Later, upon arriving in the Two Zhè regions, he was captivated by the excellence of Tiantízhù and dwelt there in a thatched hut for forty-five years.
He then traveled to Mount Mìngtiān, Mount Tāi, and various other sacred mountains until he had nearly completed his peregrinations.
In the fifteenth year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, he returned to Zhufeng. After a long time, he moved his residence to Baoyan in Pujiang.

On the first day of the first month in the second year of the Xianqing era, he molded an image with his own hands; it was completed on the ninth day and was indistinguishable from the original likeness. He then addressed his disciples, saying:
"I vowed to remain in this world for a thousand years. Since I first came to China, four hundred years have suddenly passed;
now seventy-two years have elapsed. Having spoken this verse, he entered parinirvāṇa. The world thereafter called him the "Thousand-Year Monk.

He left a testament stating that after his passing, if a monk should come to take his bones, one must not refuse. Fifty-four years later, the Elder Dafu arrived there and paid his respects at the door of the stupa.

Suddenly it opened, and he obtained its bones; they were all linked together like chains and golden in color. He therefore brought them back and constructed a separate stupa to enshrine them, establishing him as the founding patriarch of Central India. The eulogy says:
How long is human life? Like morning dew or a flowing river. From the Zhou dynasty to the Tang, my original vow has remained thus.
Waiting for Bodhidharma from the east, the Mind-Seal was finally transmitted. Who would say that the Buddha-Dharma exists only in the Western Heaven?
Tang Dynasty, Mount Jing, National Teacher No. 1, Chan Master Qin.
The Master’s name was Daoqin. He was a native of Kunshan in Wu Commandery and surnamed Zhu. His family had served in the Confucian profession for generations.

At the age of twenty-eight, he presented himself for examination at the Ministry of Rites. While traveling through Dantu, he encountered the Chan Master Xuansu of Helin and received from him the essential instructions for entering the Way.
He subsequently left the household life and attained a great realization of the fundamental tenets. After some time, he took his leave, and Xuansu said to him, “You shall go with the flow.”
Whenever he encountered a path, he would stop there. When the Master reached the foot of a mountain to the northeast of Lin’an, he asked a woodcutter for directions.
The man replied, "This is Mount Jing. The Master ascended from the northeast, traversing successive ridges until he reached the northern crag of the high peak in the west.
There he sat upon a stone bench. Suddenly, an old man dressed in white robes came before him and prostrated, saying, "I am a dragon. Since you arrived here, Master..."
"Our five hundred followers are all unsettled; we shall take our leave and return to Tianmu. We wish for this place to be the site where you plant your monk's staff.
Having spoken, they vanished. On the southern slope of Beifeng, there was a grass hut fit for habitation, which had been constructed by the dragon.

In the third year of the Dali era, Emperor Daizong issued an imperial decree summoning him to the capital, where he was received with exceptional courtesy. One day, while in the inner court, the Emperor approached and the Master rose to his feet.
The Emperor asked, "Master, why do you rise? The Master replied, "How can a donor, such as Your Majesty, presume to judge this poor monk by means of the four modes of deportment?
The Emperor was pleased and bestowed upon him the title Guoyi (National One). Over a year later, he took leave to return to Hangzhou, where he established a hermitage at his former dwelling site.
The Temple. He was the founding patriarch of this monastery. After his passing, he was posthumously honored with the title Dajue (Great Enlightenment). The eulogy states:
In every age there have been enlightened men, Emerging from among the scholars and literati. He sat in tranquil meditation at Shuangjing;
His dragon-like dwelling transformed the pearl-deep pool and its scaled-roofed houses into a sacred cloister. It became one of the nation’s namesakes; The Emperor’s bestowal was not in vain.
The Chan Master Huianzhong of Mount Daci during the Tang Dynasty was surnamed Lu and was a native of Puzhan. He possessed extraordinary features at birth, and his voice was like a bell.
He entered the monastic order at Tongzi Temple in Bingzhou and received the mind-seal from Chan Master Baizhang Hai. He then settled in a thatched hut on the southern [slope].
One day Nanquan arrived at Mount Yue’s dwelling. He asked, "What is the master of this hut? The Master said, "Heaven! Heaven!
Nanquan said, "Setting aside 'Heaven' for a moment, what is the master of this hut? The Master said, "If you understand, then you understand; do not be so talkative."
Quanshu shook his sleeves and departed. Zhaozhou asked, "What is the essence of *prajñā*? The Master replied, "What is the essence of *prajñā*? Zhaozhou laughed loudly and went out.
The next day, the Master saw Zhaozhou sweeping the ground. He asked again, "What is the essence of *prajñā*?
Zhaozhou set down his broom, clapped his hands, and laughed heartily. The Master then returned to his quarters. Later, the Master resided [at a monastery].
At Mount Daci in Zhejiang, he ascended the hall to instruct the assembly, saying: "This mountain monk cannot provide clever answers; I am only able to recognize the illness. He further said:
"To speak for ten feet is not as good as practicing for one foot; to speak for one foot is not as good as practicing for one inch. At that time, there were many students.
As the mountain was chronically short of water, the Master intended to fly his staff elsewhere. One night, he dreamed of a divine being who told him: [...the remainder of the passage...]
He said, "Do not look for it elsewhere. I shall move the Little Boy’s Spring (Xiaotongzi Quan) from South Peak here to take water from the Master.
At dawn the next day, he saw two tigers pawing at the ground with their claws; the spring gushed forth spontaneously, its flavor as sweet as molasses. A monk arrived from South Peak.
He then said, "The spring of Little Child has run dry. Thus, Dongpo inscribed a poem that says: "Stately stands the stone pagoda atop the eastern peak;
When this old man first arrived, all the spirits looked up to him. The tiger moved the spring’s source to follow his wandering feet; The dragon created ripples for his clapping hands.
To this day, when visitors have finished their ablutions, They lie listening to the sound of jade pendants on empty steps. Thus one knows this old man..."
Regarding this spring, do not harbor thoughts of coming and going in the human world. On the fifteenth day of the third month in the third year of the Xiantong era, he passed away without illness.
He was eighty-three years of age; his dharma age was fifty-four. Emperor Xizong posthumously conferred upon him the title of Great Master Xingkong and the name of the stupa, Dinghui. The eulogy says:
Trampling the path of truth, his mind awakened to the boundless. Nanquan and Zhaozhou, through their spirited exchanges and responses, dwelt there;
lacking cold spring water, the tiger ran forth to provide it for them. Thus their virtue was made manifest.
Under a clear breeze and bright sun, Master Biao of Tangxiadaku stands out.
The Master’s name was Daobiao. He was of the Qin clan of Fuyang. At the age of seven, his spirit and demeanor were exceptionally clear and flourishing.

A śramaṇa passed by and recognized his potential, encouraging him to leave the household life. In the second year of the Zhide era, an imperial decree was issued that those who could recite seven hundred sheets of Buddhist scriptures should be ordained as bhikṣus;
the Master was the first among them to be selected. Having received the tonsure, he resided at Nantianzhu Temple, where he maintained the precepts with extreme rigor. During the Yongtai era...
The abbot submitted a memorial requesting an imperial plaque for the temple’s name. He resided there for twelve years, and many of his disciples flocked to him.
He frequently constructed a thatched hall on the southern slope of Mount Lingjiu, at the foot of the Western Ridge, which he named the "Western Ridge Thatch Hall.

There he nurtured his inner spirit with ease, remaining indifferent to worldly affairs. He was particularly skilled in composing poetry; his work was refined and exquisite, ranking as a peer to Jiaoran of Wuxing and Lingche of Kuaiji.

He maintained a steady, resonant voice. His contemporaries praised him with the epithets "one who penetrates ice and snow" and "one who rubs against the clouds and the sky," and he was known as the Monk of the Western Ridge (*Xīlǐng Héshàng*).
Renowned figures of the time, such as Li Yì, Bái Jūyí, and Lù Yǔ, all held him in high esteem.
In the third year of the Chángqìng era, he passed away and was buried in the mountains. The eulogy says:

Transcending the mundane with extraordinary features, he displayed his brilliance from the time his hair was still in pigtails. Having realized the Dharma of the emptiness of karma, he lived in serene contentment, nurturing his lofty character and finding joy in poetic composition.
His style matched the elegance of the *Yajue* and the passion of the *Sao*, his fame marked the age, and he could have reached the heights of the clouds and sky—Master Yuanze of the Tang.

The Master’s name was Yuanze; he resided at Huilin Monastery and was a friend of Li Yuan, the Governor of Luoyang. They had made an agreement to travel to Mount Emei in Shu to pay homage to the Great Being Samantabhadra.
The Master wished to take the Xiyu (Slanting Valley) route, while Li Yuan wished to ascend the Gorges. The Master would not agree, but when Li Yuan insisted, they set out together.
When their boat reached Nanpu, they saw a woman wearing a brocade apron carrying a jar on her back to draw water. Upon seeing her, the Master wept.
She said, "It was for this reason that I initially did not wish to follow this path. She has been pregnant with me for three years; now that she is seen, there is no escaping it.
On the third day when the child is bathed, I pray that you will grace my gate; I shall take a smile as my token of proof."
"Twelve years hence, I shall meet you outside the Tiantzhu Monastery in Qiantang. Having finished speaking, she passed away.
Once the woman had nursed her child, Fayuan went to see her; indeed, she was smiling. He then immediately turned his boat back.
When he arrived at Tiantzhu as scheduled, beneath the mid-autumn moon, he heard a cowherd by the side of Ge Hong’s well tapping a horn and singing: "On the三生石 (Sāṃsārika Stone)..."
The spirits of the ancients—appreciating the moon and chanting in the breeze need no further discussion. I am ashamed that you, a person of feeling, have come from afar to visit me;
though this body is different, my nature remains constant. Yuan knew him to be his teacher, so he stepped forward and asked, "Master Ze, are you well?
The child said, "Lord Li is a true man of faith. My path and yours are different; do not draw near to me. Strive only in diligent cultivation. Furthermore—
The song says: "The affairs before and after this body are vast and dim; I wish to speak of their causes and conditions, yet fear it would break my heart.
Having searched through the mountains and rivers of Wu and Yue, I now turn back with my mist-shrouded oars toward Qutang. Thereupon he departed, and no one knew where he went. The eulogy says:
An appointment in the capital of Jingluo; A journey to Mount Emei. A single word before the opportune moment; Penetrating three lifetimes.
The task of drawing water from the jar was extraordinary; The poem of knocking on the horn was pure. Forever cherishing these ancient traces, The mountains are empty and the moon is bright.
—By Chan Master Tang Taoguang.

The Master’s style was Taoguang. His clan and native place are not well known. During the reign of Emperor Muzong, he thatched a hut on the western peak of Lingyin, at Chaogu Wood, where he became friends with the Venerable Linn of Niaoke.
The Prefect Bai Juyi held his Way in high esteem and once prepared a meal to entertain him, inviting him with a poem that said:
"In my humble cottage, fragrant rice is cooked, where pungent meats and strong flavors never enter. I filter spring water and purify kudzu flour; [the Master’s arrival would be a blessing.]”
Washing my hands, I pluck the wisteria flowers; the green mustard removes the yellow leaves. The red ginger bears purple sprouts.

I invite you, Master, to come and eat with me; after the meal, there is a bowl of tea. The Master replied: "This mountain monk has a rustic nature that loves forests and springs; I often rest upon the rocks at the edge of the cliffs.
I do not know how to plant pines to accompany the jade carriage, but I can only lead water to grow golden lotuses. The white clouds may for a time—"
Coming from the green ridges, the bright moon makes it difficult to descend into the azure sky. It would be unbearable for the city to witness the arrival of your flying staff;
I fear it might startle the warblers singing before the painted pavilions. Such was his lofty refinement. The hermitage was named after the Master’s title.

The Song Dynasty Chancellor, Lord Chen Yaozuo, left an inscription within the hermitage, and those who joined in the poetic exchanges were numerous. During the Shaoxing era, Feng Jie, the Junior Minister of the Court of Imperial Kinship, [visited].
A Record of the Construction of the Hermitage.
In praise, it is said: The Way is hidden within the person; The ways in which it is preserved differ. Some enter the bustling marketplaces; Others dwell in deep, lush groves.
In these shadowy nests and huts, Even governors and wardens humble themselves before them. How could this be called "concealing one's light"? It is rather like holding up the sun and moon.
Chan Master Niaoke Lin of the Tang dynasty was named Daolin.

He was of the Pan clan from Fuyang. His mother dreamed that a ray of sunlight entered her mouth and she became pregnant; at the time of his birth, an extraordinary fragrance filled the room, so he was named Xiangguang (Fragrant Light).
He left home to become a monk in his youth and went to Ximing Monastery in Chang’an to study the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Emperor Daizong issued an imperial decree [summoning him].
National Teacher Guo arrived at the imperial court. The Master (Bai Juyi) went to pay his respects to him and received the Dharma before returning south.

Upon reaching the Qinwang Mountain by West Lake, he saw a great pine tree with branches curling like a canopy; he took up residence upon it. Because of this, people of the time named the place "Bird Nest" (Wuko).

Furthermore, a magpie’s nest was situated beside it, and the birds became naturally tame and familiar with him. During the Yuanhe era, the Prefectural Governor Bai Juyi entered the mountain to visit him.
[The official] asked, "Why is your dwelling so dangerous? The Master replied, "The Governor’s situation is even more perilous.

[The official] said, "I am honored to serve as the Governor of this commandery; what danger could there be for me? The Master said, "Fuel and fire intersect, and the nature of consciousness never rests—is this not perilous?
The official was pleased and questioned him with a verse: "Having entered the Gate of Emptiness specifically to inquire of suffering and emptiness, I venture to ask about the matter of Chan..."
He called out to the Zen Master, "Is it that this dream is a matter of the floating life, or rather that the floating life is within a dream?

The Master replied, "When coming there are no tracks; when going there are no traces. The affairs of going and coming are one and the same. Why need you ask further about the matters of the floating life?
This very floating life is but a dream. His patched robes were worn through and tattered, yet he remained unchanged by cold or heat as the years passed.
He never descended from the mountain. In the fourth year of the Changqing era, he entered *nirvāṇa*. His stupa was enshrined at Xique Temple on the Northern Mountain. The eulogy says:
Leaving the perilous for the level—this is the common law of the mundane world. The ornate chambers and carved palaces have, one after another, met with ruin and collapse.
The man of ultimate realization has no fixed mind; to him, the perilous and the level are as one. If you do not believe me, the magpies nesting in the trees may serve as witness.
Chan Master Tang Zhaoxian Tong, whose name was Huìtōng, was a native of this prefecture.
His surname was Wú, and his given name was Yuánqīng. During the reign of Emperor Dēngzōng, he served as the Superintendent of the Six Palaces.
It was during the spring season when the flowers and plants were in full bloom; while he was enjoying the sights for some time, he suddenly heard a voice from the air saying: "Illusory and empty."

...its characteristics. Arising and ceasing without pause, it can destroy one's roots of goodness. How could you, O Benevolent One, look upon such a thing? Because of this, he attained great awakening.
From then on, he was suddenly filled with unease and found no joy. The Emperor, finding this strange, asked him the reason. He replied that his wish was to follow the Śākya [Buddha].

The Emperor summoned a physiognomist to examine him, saying, "This man shall succeed to the supramundane Dharma. Thereupon, he was released to return home. He went to see Tāoguang, who pointed [to him] and said:
He went to visit Niaoke to seek ordination, but after three requests, he was not granted permission. He then first built a hermitage;

once it was completed, Taoguang spoke earnestly to Niaoke on his behalf, who then shaved his head for him. He served diligently for several years without receiving the seal of transmission. One day, he took his leave.
Niaokuo asked, "Where are you going? He replied, "I am going to various places to study the Buddha-dharma. Niaokuo said, "If it is the Buddha-dharma, I have a little bit of it right here.
The monk asked, "What is the Master’s Buddha-dharma? Niaokuo plucked a tuft of cloth from his robe, held it up, and blew upon it.
At that moment, the master attained sudden and great enlightenment; thereafter, he no longer traveled elsewhere but remained constantly by Niaokuo’s side.
In the world he was known as the "Cotton-Fluff Attendant. This Zhaoxian Temple is the very site where the Master practiced his Way. The eulogy says:

With the rank of a golden pheasant official close to the Purple Forbidden City, The spring air was thick with splendor. Yet he severed and abandoned wealth and honor, Vanishing as swiftly as a light swan.
Seeking a teacher and yearning for the Way, He bore toil and hardship upon his person. Had he not possessed wisdom and courage, How could he have awakened to True Emptiness?
The Tang Dynasty Chan Master Wuzhuo Xixi, whose name was Wenxi, was a native of Yuer Creek in Jiahe. His surname was Zhu. He received full ordination during the Kaiyuan era.

Initially, he studied the *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya) and concurrently lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra*. He frequently traveled to Mount Wutai to pay homage to the Great Being Mañjuśrī. One night, he arrived at...
At an ancient temple, he encountered an old monk and asked about the state of the Buddha-dharma and the number of the assembly in the South.

After the Master had answered all these questions, he in turn asked, "How is the Buddha-dharma maintained here? The monk replied, "Dragons and snakes are intermingled; ordinary people and sages dwell together. He further asked, "How many are in the assembly?
The monk said, "Three before three, three after three. The Master was left perplexed. When the tea was finished, he ordered a youth—
He was sent out the gate, whereupon he suddenly vanished; there remained only high forests and deep valleys. Later, he studied under Yangshan and attained awakening.
Yangshan appointed him as the head cook (*dianzuo*). One day, seeing Mañjuśrī riding a lion by the side of the stove, the Master rebuked him, saying, "Mañjuśrī is Mañjuśrī;
Wenxi is Wenxi. He then struck him with his palm. Mañjuśrī surged into the air and said, "The bitter gourd is attached..."
The root is bitter; yet the melon is sweet all the way through to the stem. Having practiced for three great kalpas, he was nevertheless disparaged by this old monk.
During the Xiántóng era, he built a dwelling and lived in retirement on Mount Qiānqǐng. In the third year of the Guāngqì era, Qian Wǔsù Wáng invited him to reside at Cíguāng Yuàn in Yúháng.
An imperial edict granted him purple robes and the title "Wúzhù. In the third year of the Guānghuà era, he moved to reside at Wúzhù Yuàn. This is [the account].
In the middle of a winter night, he addressed the assembly, saying, "The exhaustion of the mind within the three realms is itself nirvana. He then sat in the lotus posture and passed away.
At that time, a white light emanated from the abbot’s quarters, hanging down from the trees and becoming one with their color. A stupa was erected in the western valley of Lingyin. The eulogy says:
Before seeing Yangshan, he was sold on Mount Wutai; Once he has seen Yangshan, what need is there for the labor of the "Snail-Object" (Yuan Nai)?
Rare things are seldom considered marvelous; Frequent invitations from guests provoke resentment. "Ugh! Ugh! Mañjuśrī! The grass-robber has defeated himself.
Master Baiyun Yi of the Five Dynasties.
The Master’s name was Daoyi. It is unknown where he was from. In the fourth year of the Tiānfú era of the Shí Jìn dynasty (937 CE), he erected a hermitage on the northwest side of Mount Tiānzhú.
Clad in grass and subsisting on wood, his noble conduct transcended the mundane. One night, he saw a light illuminating the heavens atop the peak before him.
Following its source, he looked and discovered a wondrous tree that no one could identify. The Master then took it and commanded—
The artisan Kong Renqian carved it into an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. One night, he dreamed of a person in white robes who said, "The statue is now complete.
Tomorrow, a monk will come from Luoyang carrying ancient Buddha relics; you should seek them."
Shortly thereafter, the monk Guo arrived. Following his dream, they sought him out and obtained three *śarīra* relics, which were enshrined within the crown of the Great Being’s head.
From that time on, his spiritual manifestations became widely renowned. During the Wuyue period, King Zhongyi first renovated the monastery grounds and honored him there.
In the Tiānshèng era of the Song dynasty, the two monks Chōng and Jì further relocated the hall to the southeast, directly facing Rǔdòu Peak. [This occurred during the] Zhìpíng era.

In the second year [of the reign], Lord Cai Xiang, the Prefectural Governor, memorialized the Emperor regarding this matter. Duke Zeng submitted a petition and was granted the plaque title "Linggan Guanyin Monastery. The eulogy states:
"The light of the Great Being’s mind Is mysteriously manifested in this wood; Why do the multitudes not see it? It is because their minds do not respond."
The Master’s mind was the Buddha-mind; their same essence was manifest. Appearing in the body of a layman, he brought eternal blessing to the imperial lineage for five generations.
The Reverend Ear-Phase (Ear-Shape) was named Xingxiu and styled Fazhen.
He was of the Chen clan of Southern Quanzhou. His family had long been a prominent and wealthy house, and they adhered to Confucian learning; yet the Master alone...
He maintained a pure mind and took no pleasure in remaining in secular life. At thirteen, he left the household life and traveled extensively to visit masters in various regions.

He received the Dharma from Chan Master Cunen of Xuefeng. From birth, the Master possessed extraordinary features: his ears hung down to his shoulders, extending upward beyond the crown of his head and downward to his chin.
He was thus known at the time as "The Long-Eared Monk. In the second year of the Tiānchéng era of the Later Táng dynasty, he departed from Guǐqīng Temple on Mount Tiāntái.
Yanyou traveled to Qiantang, where the King of Wuyue received him with the etiquette due to a guest. He resided at Faxiang Monastery on South Mountain.

He was accustomed to soliciting people to perform meritorious deeds (*puṇya*). Someone once asked the Master, "I do not understand what form or substance there is in a master's solicitation for people to perform meritorious deeds.

The Master replied, "It can conceal a hundred uglinesses. On the second day of the middle winter month in the fourth year of Qianguo, the Qian family held a vegetarian feast for the monks to celebrate his birthday.
He asked Yongming, "Is there a holy monk in this assembly? Yongming replied, "The Venerable Long-ear is an emanation of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara.
Subsequently, Yongming instructed his attendant in advance, saying, "If the Long-ear one comes, simply tell him that I am sleeping.
When the Master approached Yongming, the attendant followed the instructions and informed him. The Master then took Yongming’s leather sandals and covered himself with them.
He returned and passed away while sitting in meditation the following day. His disciples lacquered his entire body, which remains preserved to this day.
In the second year of the Chongning era, he was posthumously granted the title of Great Master Chonghui. The eulogy states:
The Buddha, for the sake of all living beings, possesses immeasurable vows of compassion; manifesting his transformation body to spread blessings, he appears as a bridge and raft for the world.
Bearing the marks of a Great Man, with earrings suspended from both ears, Yongming Youyu was the Chan Master Yongming Qian of the fifth generation of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.

The Master’s name was Daoyan; he was a native of Hexun Prefecture and surnamed Wu. Initially, he visited Qingliang Fayan, who, upon seeing him, marveled at his extraordinary character and granted him permission to enter the inner quarters.
One day, Fayan asked him, "Aside from your formal inquiries and requests for instruction, what sutra are you currently studying? The Master replied, "The Avatamsaka Sutra."
Fayan asked, "Under which category are the six characteristics—totality, particularity, sameness, difference, formation, and disintegration—subsumed?

The Master replied, "All phenomena, both mundane and supramundane, are fully endowed with these six characteristics. Fayan asked, "Does emptiness also possess the six characteristics? The Master was unable to answer.
Fayan said, "Ask me this question instead. The Master asked as he had been told. Fayan replied, "Empty.
At these words, the Master attained awakening. Fayan asked, "How do you understand this? The Master said, "Empty. Fayan approved.

Later, when a crowd of fourfold assemblies—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—entered the temple, Fayan said, "The Vinaya states that if one hears the sound of hairpins and bracelets from across a wall, it is called breaking the precepts."
"Now I see gold, silver, and robes of crimson and purple gathered together; is this breaking the precepts? The Master said, "A fine way in.

Fayan said, "In the future, you will have five hundred disciples, and you shall be held in high esteem by kings and lords. The Master then took his leave and went to an old temple in Sangu to read the Tripitaka.
King Qian Zhongyi summoned him to the palace to receive the Bodhisattva Precepts and appointed him as [Director of] Ci... (the title is abbreviated).

He transformed the name [of the monastery] into Dinghui (Wisdom and Samādhi). In the first year of the Xiande era of the Zhou dynasty, he established Huiriji Yongming Monastery and invited the Master to reside there as its founding patriarch.
His community regularly numbered five hundred, which truly fulfilled the prediction of Fayan. When the Song dynasty arrived, Yongming was renamed Jingci. The eulogy says:

A towering vessel of the Dharma, Nurturing spiritual brilliance from the rivers and mountains of Song; The empty flowers manifesting the Avataṃsaka’s marks, Heir to the lineage of the Eye of the Dharma.
His fame resounded through the imperial capital, Where the jade-crested sovereign paid him profound respect. Under the ancestral command of Yongming, He was like the brilliant sun rising in the sky.
—Master Zhijue Shou of the Five Dynasties Period.

The Master’s name was Yanshou, his courtesy name was Chongyuan, and he was of the Wang clan of Yuhang. In his youth, he served as the military commander of Huating; because he used official funds to release captive animals, he was sentenced to death.
When he was led to the marketplace for execution, his countenance remained unchanged. King Wenmu marveled at this and granted him permission to leave the household life.

He resided at Longce Monastery, where he performed manual labor to provide for the community and maintained a single meal a day, sitting constantly without lying down. He received the Dharma from Tiantai.

National Teacher Shao initially resided at Xuedou. He subsequently returned to West Lake. In the second year of the Jianlong era, King Zhongyi invited him to serve as the second patriarch of Yongming.
He remained there for fifteen years, during which his assembly consistently numbered two thousand. He was bestowed the title Zhijue and later moved to Tiantai.

In his dwelling, he practiced giving food at night and releasing living beings in the morning. Six times a day, he scattered flowers and practiced the Way, reciting one hundred and eight items daily without ever failing for even a moment.
With whatever energy remained, he chanted the *Lotus Sūtra*, totaling thirteen thousand fascicles. He was also known by the sobriquet Baoyizi (Child Embracing Oneness).
Previously, while in meditative contemplation, the Master had been graced by the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, who poured nectar into his mouth, whereby he attained great...

Diancai (Biàn Tài). He composed the *Zongjing Lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source) in one hundred and twenty fascicles to reconcile the divergences between the Tiantai, Xianshou, and Cien schools.
His poems and gāthās numbered several million words and were disseminated abroad;
the King of Goryeo sent a letter acknowledging him as his teacher and presented him with a robe woven of gold thread, a rosary of amethyst, and a golden ritual pitcher. He opened...
He passed away in the eighth year of the Baoyu era and was interred in a stupa at Jingci Mountain. The eulogy says:
The Buddha has no divergent teachings, yet the choices of his followers differ. I take up a single mirror to reflect those three schools.
Irrigated by the nectar of the Dharma, their profound currents are inexhaustible. It is fitting that even in foreign lands, all should turn toward this wind with one accord.
During the Five Dynasties period, there was the Chan Master Wuyun Feng (also known as Zhifeng).
A native of Yuhang, he was naturally averse to meat from birth, and his skin and body were fragrant and pure.

He left the household life at Mount Dongsan in Lin’an and became thoroughly versed in the Three Studies. During the Tianfu era of the Jin dynasty, he studied under National Teacher Shaokang of Tiantai and attained awakening.
One day, he entered the Samantabhadra Hall and sat in meditative repose. Suddenly, a divine being knelt before him with knees bent.
The Master asked, "Who are you? He replied, "I am a guardian deity of the precepts. The Master said, "I fear that my past transgressions have not yet been extinguished;

do you know of them? He replied, "What sins does the Master have? There is only a minor oversight. The Master asked, "What is it? He replied, "Whenever you pour out water from your bowl, that water is also the property of a donor. The Master..."
"He always discards it; this is not appropriate. Having finished speaking, he vanished. From then on, the Master drank all of it.

When the Kings of Wu and Yue heard his reputation, they bestowed upon him the purple robe and summoned him to grant him the title Pujue. They commanded him to reside at Gongchen Mountain. At the beginning of the Kaibao era, [the Emperor]...
When King Zhongyi established Pumen Jingshe Monastery, he invited [Zhi]yang to expound the essentials of the school and serve as its founding patriarch.

After four years, [Zhi]yang declined the post on account of his old age. At that time, the general Ling Chao offered him the newly constructed Huayan Doctrinal Center at Mount Wuyun as a place for his final years.
Whenever he went out, he carried a large fan; he would beg for money to buy meat to feed the tigers, who would always come to meet him.
He was carried back to the mountain. In the second year of the Yongxi era, he passed away. The eulogy says:
"The taste of meat and blood was something he had never known since birth. The tiger, unable to find flesh, seemed as if it were appeasing its own hunger;
it trailed its tail from the forest, welcomed him as he was being carried home. Who would say these were different species? They shared a single mechanism of transformation."
Chan Master Yuan of Mount Gu at Song was named Zhìyuán;

his courtesy name was Wúwài. He was of the Xù clan of Qiántáng. He entered the monastic order at the age of eight and received the transmission of the Three Contemplations of Tiantai from Fèngxiān Yuánqīng.
The Master once lamented that since the passing of Jīngxī, subtle teachings had fallen into ruin; he therefore devoted himself to them.

He composed ten commentaries to elucidate the sutras. From an early age, the Master was diligent in Confucian studies and also delved into the works of Laozi and Zhuangzi; he styled himself "The Son of the Doctrine of the Mean" (Zhongyongzi).
Residing at the Maṇi Monastery on Mount Gu, he maintained a high standard of integrity that transcended the mundane world.

When Wang Wenmu, having resigned from the相位 (prime minister), came to govern the prefecture, all the monks went out beyond the pass to welcome him. Ciyun sent a messenger to invite the Master to accompany them, but the Master declined on account of illness, smiling as he did so.
He said to the messenger, "Convey my regards to Ciyun: let one monk remain at Qiantang for the time being. Those who heard this sighed in admiration.
From his youth, the Master had suffered from chronic illness and mostly kept to his door, living in solitude; he was a neighbor and friend only to Lin Bu of Chuzhou.
Xianghao amused himself with poetry and prose, composing fifty-one scrolls of miscellaneous writings titled *The Collection of Leisurely Dwelling* (*Xiánjū biān*).
On the seventeenth day of the second month in the first year of the Qiànxìng era, he composed his own funeral oration and elegies. Two days later, he passed away.
His disciples followed his final instructions to carve out a tomb behind the mountain of the monastery; they enshrined him in earthenware vessels and interred them together. Fifteen years later...

After heavy rains, the mountain collapsed and exposed the Master’s reliquary chamber. His true body was found uncorrupted; his nails and hair had grown long, his lips were slightly parted, and his teeth were as white as jade or snow.
He was posthumously titled Fahui (Dharma-Wisdom). In the second year of the Zhiping era, the name of the temple was changed to Baosheng Yuan.

In the twenty-first year of the Shaoxing era, the Yanxiang Guan was established there. The authorities renovated the Master’s residence to expand it and moved the plaque to the northern side of the mountain.
The pagoda was moved and enshrined therein. The eulogy says: A swan’s down values power;
a cicada sheds the clamor of the dust. Upon a single, frail couch, with layered scrolls and flying brushstrokes, Stands firm the solitary mountain;
amidst the forest clouds, all is silent and desolate. Though the traces have been erased, its height remains unlevelled.
Master Ciyun Shi of the Song dynasty, whose name was Zunshe and courtesy name Zhibai, was of the Ye clan of Ninghai in Taizhou. His mother dreamed of swallowing a bright pearl before he was born.

He left the household life at Dongye Mountain and transmitted the Tiantai teachings to Master Baoyun Tong. Before long, he succeeded him on the Dharma seat. In the eighth year of the Xiangfu era, Prefectural Governor Mr.
Xue invited him to reside at Ling Shan Tianzhu Monastery. As the monastery had long been in ruins, the Master restored it according to its former layout.
When Minister Wang Wenmu was appointed as local governor, he held the Master’s Way in high esteem and memorialized the throne to restore the name "Tianzhu. Shortly thereafter...
He requested the bestowal of the title "Ciyun" (Cloud of Compassion). Empress Dowager Zhangxian dispatched an envoy bearing white gold to command him to perform repentance rites.

The Master composed the *Jinguangming Huguo Yiwen* (The Ritual Text for the Golden Light Sutra’s Protection of the Nation) and presented it to the throne. He subsequently petitioned that the Tiantai doctrinal texts be included in the Tripitaka.

Furthermore, based on the sutras, he compiled various repentance methods that became widely prevalent in the world. He regularly practiced samādhi, setting a period of ninety days as his term. The Master...
He practiced these with vigor, and his spiritual responses were manifold; whatever prayers he offered for the sake of the Dharma invariably came to pass. He maintained only three principles.
Furthermore, when constructing the Gwangmyeong (Light) Repentance Hall, for every rafter and every brick laid, he would invariably recite the Great Compassion Mantra seven times.

Though it has repeatedly suffered from the ravages of war and fire, it stands alone, towering and intact—this was due to the power of his vows. The Master’s poetry and prose were elegant and refined; he authored the *Ginyeon* (Golden Garden) and *Yingwon* (Spiritual Garden).
The *Tianzhu bieji* (Separate Collection from India) records that in the ninth year of the Tiānshèng era, he returned to the Cāotáng Hermitage on Mount Dōnglǐng.

On the night of the eighteenth day of the tenth month of the following year, a great star fell upon the mountain, and the Master entered nirvana. He was posthumously conferred the honorary titles Fǎbǎo Chánhuì (Dharma-Jewel, Chan-Wisdom). In the eighth year of the Chún yòu era...
His disciple Ming-yin prayed for clear weather and obtained a response. The Emperor inscribed a calligraphic edict and added the posthumous title "Shengying" (Sacred Response).

In the eleventh year of the Chunyou era, Ming-yin again prayed for clear weather and once more obtained a response. The Emperor inscribed another calligraphic edict and added the posthumous title "Zhengjue" (Correct Enlightenment). The eulogy says:
The single school of Tailing flourished through Fazhi; the Master emerged from Baoyun.

Like elder brothers of gold and younger brothers of jade, they manifested the patience of non-arising, dwelt upon the stage of non-retrogression, and were repeatedly honored with illustrious titles that have never fallen into oblivion throughout antiquity—Song Mingjiao Chanshi Song.
The Master’s name was Qisong, his courtesy name Zhongling. He was a native of Tanjin in Tengzhou and belonged to the Li clan. He entered the monastic order at the age of seven;

having received full ordination, he habitually wore an image of the Holy Avalokiteśvara and recited its name ten thousand times daily. There were no scriptures, commentaries, or miscellaneous books that he did not memorize extensively.
Having received the Dharma from Master Cong of Dongshan, he arrived in Qiantang during the Qingli era and took delight in the lakes and mountains.
Having found this place superior, he finally halted his carriage there. He styled himself Qianzi (the Hidden Master). In a solitary room, he lived in serene seclusion;

closing his door, he composed writings, producing the *Fujiao lun* (Treatise on Assisting the Teachings) in over one hundred thousand words, clarifying the unity of Confucianism and Buddhism. He also authored the *Dingzu tu* (Chart of the Fixed Patriarchs) and the *Zhengzong ji* (Record of the True Lineage).

Carrying these works with him, he entered the capital and presented them through Wang Gong Su, the Imperial Archivist and Governor of the Prefecture. Emperor Renzong praised them with deep admiration.

An imperial edict was issued to entrust him to the Translation Court (Chuanfa Yuan) for the compilation of his works; he was honored with the title "Enlightened Teaching" (Mingjiao), and his writings were granted entry into the Tripitaka.
Both Duke Han Zhongxian and Duke Ou Yang Wenzhong praised him, whereby his fame resounded throughout the realm.

Subsequently, he returned to the East, where he was invited to reside at Mount Furi by Lord Cai Xiang, who served as the local governor. After several years there, he retired to live out his final years at Lingyin.
At the Yong’an Vihāra, he manifested parinirvāṇa in the fifth year of the Xīníng era. Upon cremation, three of his six sense organs remained unimpaired:
the eyes, the tongue, and the *kumārabhūta* (the crown of the head). Together with his cranial bone and a rosary, these five items were preserved.

The śarīras that emerged were brilliant red and white, pure and lustrous, shaped like large soybeans. He was interred to the left of the Yong’an Temple. His disciples compiled his writings, entitled the *Tán*.
Collected at Jin. The eulogy says:
Shutting his door to compose his writings, He draws from antiquity and connects with the present. Unveiling his sincerity before the imperial palace, His true spirit stands in dense array.
His fame spreads across the seas and the earth; His Way vibrates through the Zen groves. Unwasted even after a hundred refinements— This manifests the essence of pure gold.
Master Zhenguankan of the Song dynasty was named Yunkan.
A native of Qiantang, at the age of nine, a guest pointed to a young cassia tree to test him;

he replied, "Just born on the slopes of the rocky valley, it already possesses the fragrance of the moon. He was erudite and profoundly learned, and he compiled the Twelve Sections of the Vinaya Canon.
He was proficient in the commentaries on the sutras and treatises, as well as in writings such as the prefaces to the *Dharmamukha-zaṅ* (Verses on the Gateways to the Dharma).

In the seventh year of the Qingli era, he was granted the title Great Master Zhenwu. During the Chongning era, his posthumous title was augmented to Zhìyuán. Chen Shunyú of Jiahe composed a record of his life and deeds (*xíngyèjì*).
He was initially interred at Yongquan Mountain on West Lake; later, his stupa was moved to West Lake. The eulogy says:
The Threefold Training in the Outflows-Free, with Precepts as the Foremost; The Sage does not arise again—whose lineage shall transmit it?
I take up my brush to compose this record, to propagate the model for humans and devas. Silent through the ages, the Precious Moon hangs high.
Chan Master Shanzheng of Mount Gongchen, Meritorious Official of the Song Dynasty.
The Master’s name was Weizheng, his courtesy name was Huanyan, and he was of the Huang family of Huating. From childhood, he possessed extraordinary insight.
At eighteen, he received full ordination and immediately began traveling to seek the Way for thirty years. Upon concluding his period of study, he resided at the Jingtu Monastery on Mount Gongchen.
Whenever he traveled, he would habitually ride a yellow ox. During the Qingli era, Minister of State Jiang Tang was close friends with the Master; he once presented him with a poem that said:
"Zen guests regularly enter the old capital; a yellow ox's horn bears a water jar and bowl. Sometimes, donning a rain hat, he goes through the clouds;
it would be well to paint a picture together with the clouds. This is a factual record. Someone asked the Master, "Why do you not speak of Chan? He replied:
To waste words is idle; I am too weary to take the trouble of elaborate detail. I merely cause the myriad phenomena to unfold their exposition day and night.
By nature, I am simple and straightforward; in winter I do not use a brazier, but instead make balls of reed flowers and tuck my feet within them. When guests arrive, we share this together.
He took particular delight in gazing at the moon. Every time he sat cross-legged in a large basin floating upon a pond, he would turn it himself, chanting and whistling until dawn;
this was his regular practice. His poetry was sharp and striking, its conceptual depth exceedingly high. One day, Master Jiang said, "Tomorrow there is a banquet for guests at the Prefectural Office.
I have prepared a separate vegetarian feast to invite you, Master; I hope you will join me for some pure conversation. The Master consented. The next day, he left behind one...
He departed with a verse, which said: "Yesterday was once today; as I step out the gate leaning on my staff, I reflect again.
As a monk, one ought to dwell among crags and valleys; it is truly unsuitable for a state official at this banquet. Furthermore, a verse from the mountains says:
"Ten thousand peaks above the bridge, a thousand miles of water below. Only the white egret sees me come here so often. [Then he] sent [this verse]:
The monk’s verse says: What is there within the mountains? Upon the ridges, many white clouds. They can only bring solace to oneself;
They cannot be taken to present to you. He often praised his own portrait, saying: Ancient features and slender form, leaning on a staff of *lǐ* wood. Clearly painted is Subhūti.
Understanding emptiness does not permit departing from sound and form; It seems as though one hears a solitary monkey crying under the moon. All people transmitted [this].
He recited [the scriptures]. His calligraphy possessed the style of the Jin masters. Qin Shaoyou especially cherished and played with it;
whenever he saw his brushwork, he would invariably take it to collect. The world called him "Zheng Huangniu. The eulogy says:
His lofty air transcends the mundane; his pure chanting leaves the dust behind. With a single straw hat upon his ox’s back, he dwells among the woods and by the waterside.
His appearance is emaciated and his manner is simple; one cannot approach him intimately. How does he find delight for himself?
Amidst the white clouds on the ridges—thus spoke the Dharma Master Bian of Songhae.
The Master’s name was Huibian; his courtesy name was Nuweng. He was the son of the Fu family of Huating.

He received his formal training at Puzhao Monastery and studied the Tiantai teachings and contemplations under Tianzhu Shaorou and Fushui Ju. When Shaorou was nearing the end of his life, he charged the Master with lecturing in his stead.

Shaorou had a dream in which Zhanran struck his mouth with a golden probe and said, "If you are diligent in instructing others, you shall attain discerning wisdom. After a long time, [the Master] succeeded him.
During the Jiayou era, when Shen Gong Gou of the Hanlin Academy was the regional governor, he governed with strictness.

Observing Master Shi’s conduct, he found him uniquely outstanding and appointed him to a monastic office, subsequently promoting him to the position of Capital Monastic Rectifier (*duisengzheng*). At that time, Su Dongpo served as the local Vice-Governor and often engaged in spiritual exchanges with the Master.
For twenty-five years, they lectured and taught together, with a constant following of over a thousand people. Not long after, the Master retired to live in seclusion in the grasses.
The Hall. He simply maintained six matters throughout his life. In the winter of the sixth year of the Xīníng era, he rose at dawn, washed himself, and passed away apart from the assembly.
His final instruction was that the coffin must not be closed until Sōngpō arrived. On the fourth day, Sōngpō finally reached the mountain;
he saw him sitting cross-legged as if alive, with the crown of his head still warm. He composed three quatrains in the *jié* style to mourn him. Twenty-one years had passed since the Master’s death.
Dongpo wrote a postscript recounting these events: "After I left Hangzhou, I dreamed that I arrived at West Lake where there was a great hall with a plaque inscribed 'The Descent of Maitreya.
My old friend, Master Bian Haoyue, and others were all practicing the Way within it.
I then composed a hymn of praise, and Yingbin inscribed his epitaph for his stupa. The hymn says:"
A solitary moon over the vast blue sea, Born amidst the clouds; The flying wheel atop Mount Zhu, Where all phenomena are chilled by its light.
Who knows this? The old immortal of Mei Mountain. If you do not believe it, Then these inscriptions and praises are as clear as the bright moon.
—By the Song Dynasty Master Biancai Jing.
The Master’s name was Yuánjìng; his courtesy name was Wúxiàng. He was of the Xú clan of Yúqián. At birth, a fleshy protuberance rose on his left shoulder like the folds of a *kāṣāya* robe;
it disappeared after eighty-one days. His father sighed and said, "This child is a śramaṇa from a previous life. He entered the monastic order as a youth.
He received his training under Ciyun, practicing with diligent effort day and night. After Ciyun passed away, he further served Mingzhi.

At the age of twenty-five, he was granted purple robes and the title "Biancai" (Eloquent Talent). Prefect Shen Gong Gou remarked that the Upper Tianzhu Avalokiteśvara Sanctuary used vocal repentance as its primary Buddhist practice, rather than as a dwelling for *dhyāna* meditation.
He requested that the Master replace this with the teachings [of the Tiantai school]. The Master...
Upon his arrival, people from Wu and Yue vied with one another to come; they excavated the mountain and added chambers until nearly ten thousand pillars were erected.

The number of students increased several-fold. In the seventeenth year, there was one who sought to seize [the monastery] for profit; however, after more than a year, the usurper met with defeat. The Master was reinstated as the abbot. Zhao Qingxian Gong praised him, saying:
"When the Master departed from Tiantai, the mountains became desolate and the ghosts wailed. When the Master returned to Tiantai, the site of the Dharma assembly shone with brilliance. After two...
In his later years, he retired to the Dragon Well on South Mountain. Throughout his life, he had diligently cultivated the Pure Land practice;

his realization was perfected and his power fully established, such that the manifestations of his attainment were manifold. Once, while eating with the monk Xi Zhong, the latter observed a light like a firefly between the Master’s eyebrows;
reaching out to grasp it, he obtained a *śarīra*. Subsequently, *śarīra* were frequently found at the places where he slept or arose. (The year) Yuanyou 8...
He passed away at the age of eighty-one, thus fulfilling the omen of the birthmark on his shoulder.
When his stupa was completed, Dongpo recorded his life and deeds, and Yingbin composed the inscription. The eulogy reads:
The Dharma Garden is about to flourish; its pillars and beams depend upon you. As you sweep away the white clouds with your whisk, fragrant rain falls in profusion.
From Zhao to Su, you shall surely follow these lofty footsteps. At Longjing, the breeze is pure; all who pass by must be solemn.
—By the Dharma Master Zhen of Nanping, Song Dynasty.
The Master’s name was Daozhen. He transmitted the teachings of Fazhi of Siming.

Initially residing at Longyou on Mount Jinshan, he was invited by Wu Gong—the Vice Governor of the capital—who had heard of his reputation, to take charge of the Xingjiao Chan Monastery. Students flocked to him from all quarters.

Whenever the Master lectured, he would compile and synthesize the meanings of the texts, penetrating them from beginning to end. It was from Nanping that the Tiantai school of study in Western Zhejiang first began to flourish greatly.
I once composed two verses in praise of the *Miaozongchao* (Commentary on the Miaozong): "The Buddha permitted the six levels of realization to distinguish [the stages];
why then does the dung beetle not understand this? To know the one but not the two is to lose the West and lose the East as well. If the 'Thirty' were truly established, all would be eternal bliss;

Yet the dung beetle does not reach the ultimate, for the Buddhas have severed inherent evil. Later, I debated the gates of the teachings with Master Jingjue Yue, presenting my arguments as follows: [text continues]
The officials requested that a high platform be built and a red banner erected, imitating the holy masters of Western India who competed for victory against non-Buddhists;

they proposed that the banner mark the site of the debate, and that those whose arguments fell into error be beheaded or have their tongues cut off and hung there. The Prefect of the Commandery, Du, prohibited this and would not comply, causing all who heard of it to feel a sense of awe.

Initially, whenever Lord Wu was available during his days of leave, he would request a lecture; he would wear his formal robes and wait outside the gate, never entering until the Master had ascended the platform.
He would not enter the hall abruptly. Dongpo said: "When I was conversing with him in a large assembly, there were things I had forgotten;
the Master would then recite them for me from memory, flowing on without ceasing. In the memorial for Biancai, Dongpo wrote: "Jiang Youbian Zhen" refers to this very Master.
During the Chongning era, he was posthumously titled Shixiang (True Aspect). The eulogy states:
To the south lies a mountain, A jade screen set by Heaven. The Master preached beneath it, And ghosts and spirits came to hear the Dharma.
His valor in debate was such that his spirit could command a thousand soldiers; His words remain undiminished, Still serving as a model for posterity.
—By Vinaya Master Dazhizhao of the Song Dynasty.

The Master’s name was Yuanzhao, his courtesy name was Zhanran, and he was of the Tang family from Yuhang. In his youth, he relied upon Master Huijian of the Eastern Library at Xiangfu Temple to study the Vinaya.

Upon meeting Master Shenwu Qian, who was lecturing on the Tiantai teachings and contemplations, he followed him as a disciple, exhaustively investigating the various schools of thought while taking the Vinaya as his foundation.
He further received the Bodhisattva precepts from Master Guangci, whereupon the radiance of his precepts manifested suddenly.
Gradually, he became fully equipped with all the Vinaya disciplines. The Nanshan school flourished and was greatly revitalized by him.

He constantly wore the *kāṣāya* robe, carried his staff and bowl, and went to the marketplace to beg for food. Yang Wuweiz praised him, saying: "He goes out carrying his bowl; he returns carrying his bowl."

The Buddha-mind is ever-present during the four modes of deportment. When he first entered the marketplace, people did not recognize him; yet the void is always there, and spirits and deities know it.
He presided over monastic seats in four prefectures and later resided at Lingzhi for thirty years. His assembly regularly numbered several hundred. He once said:

"To transform the present age, nothing is better than lecturing and expounding the Dharma; to provide for the future, nothing is better than composing written works. Thus, he compiled the *Zizhi*, the *Jiyuan*, and the *Xingzong*.

He compiled over one hundred fascicles, including the *Yingfa zhufa baoen zhiji* (Record of Responses on Repaying the Kindness of Abiding in the Dharma According to the Dharma), the *Shiliu guan xiao Mituo yishu* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Shorter Amitābha Sūtra’s Sixteen Contemplations), and a revised edition of the *Vinaya*.
He also authored twenty fascicles of the *Zhiyuan ji* (Collection from the Garden of Wisdom). He styled himself the "Son of Peaceful Patience" (*Anrenzi*).

In the autumn of the sixth year of the Zhenghe era, he was commissioned to recite the *Bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna*; he then passed away while sitting cross-legged. Fishermen all heard the sound of celestial music.
A stupa was erected to the northwest of Lingzhi. His posthumous title was "Dazhi" (Great Wisdom). The eulogy says:
The secret treasury of the Vinaya was renowned at Zhongnan; When it declined in the interim, who could revitalize it?

Dazhi arose in majesty. His conduct harmonized with the myriad practices; He compiled the treatises of all vehicles. He departed westward toward the Garden of Lingzhi; Celestial music came to welcome him.

The Tripitaka Master Daofa of the Song Dynasty was named Fadao (formerly named Yongdao). He was of the Mao clan of Shunchang. Having left the household life, he took the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Śata-dharmaka-śāstra* as his primary studies.
Furthermore, he received the esoteric mantras and ritual manuals of the Tripiṭaka from Yao Tianzong, and transmitted the Perfect and Sudden Precepts (*yuantun jiefǎ*) to Yuan.

Master Zhao mastered all their essential points. During the Zhenghe era, he was granted purple robes and appointed as the head of Xiangji Monastery in the Left Street. He was bestowed the title Baojue.

When Lin Lingsu deceived the Emperor with heterodox teachings, an edict was issued at the beginning of the Xuande era to change the name of monks to "Virtuous Scholars" (Deshi) and require them to wear caps and gowns;

throughout the empire, everyone followed this without daring to lag behind. The Master alone remained steadfast and defiantly resisted the decree, resulting in his being branded and exiled to Daozhou. Later...
In the seventh year [of the Jiading era], he returned to the monastic community. In the third year of the Jianyan era, he was granted the title Yuan Tong Fa Ji.

During the Shaoxing era, he was summoned for an audience. The Emperor wished to remove the ink-stains from his eyebrows, but the Master said, "Although I am grateful for Your Majesty’s grace, I cannot bear to erase the ink of the late Emperor.
The Emperor remarked, "This monk remains stubborn to the end; it is simply a matter of following his own convenience. According to established custom, monks at the Daochang...
From the Chongguan era onward, the old regulations were changed so that the left was for heterodox paths and the right for the orthodox.

The Master could not tolerate this and went to the imperial court to debate with the Daoist Liu Ruqian; he ultimately succeeded in having the matter rectified. In the autumn of the seventeenth year, he sat upright and passed away while reciting a verse.
The cremation was performed, and his relics were innumerable. A stupa was erected at Jiu-li Song. The eulogy says:
Since ancient times, the sages of the Way Have sacrificed their bodies for the sake of the Dharma. Now that the body has perished, What need is there to speak of nirvana?
In these barbarian lands, the miasma is heavy; Yet the grace of the Imperial Throne is new. To view all things as equal and without obstruction— Like floating clouds across the vast void.

In the Northern Pass of Song, there was the Vinaya Master named Siming Jingxing, whose secular surname was Yu and who hailed from Qiantang. He was skilled at painting Amitābha Buddha and reached a level of exquisite mastery;
Yang Wuweishi called him "Yu-Mituo" (Yu-Amitābha), and this became his popular name. Having renounced his home to study Buddhism, he took up residence in a rented house in the Northern Pass.
He provided meals for the monastic community; before twenty years had passed, the number reached three million.

He then moved the plaque of Miaoxing Temple and expanded his residence into a monastery, which continues to provide hospitality without interruption to this day. During the period of civil unrest, the temple alone was not burned.

When the master encountered a rebel camp, he vowed to sacrifice his own life in exchange for the lives of the entire city; the rebels were struck with awe and consequently refrained from their depredations. Someone once asked the master if he could paint an image of Amitābha.
"Why do you not practice Chan? The Master replied, "Throughout my life, I have only known how to recite the name of Amitābha; I do not know how to practice Chan—what can be done?
As long as the wind and moon remain over the Five Lakes, what need is there to brandish weapons in times of peace?

When the Master was a child, he used to visit Duobao Mountain on West Lake and would often make a vow, saying, "In the future, I shall carve this rock into a Buddha. Later, he indeed did so for Maitreya.
Regarding the Maitreya statue: When Attendant Xue Gong asked, "Maitreya is currently preaching the Dharma in the heavenly palace;

why carve [this image] out of stone? the Master replied, "Alas, you stubborn stone! It relies entirely upon the skillful artisan. Right now is Maitreya Buddha; do not wait for his descent to seek him.
Such was the Master’s spontaneous and responsive manner of answering. Throughout his life, the Master was dedicated to substance and did not engage in empty ornamentation. He succeeded...
In the winter of the seventh year of the Xing period, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. Minister Zhang Jiucheng (Wugou) inscribed his stupa, praising him with these words:
"Forever liberated from the dust of the world, Not turning according to external things; The Amitābha that is inherently present Is manifested upon the tip of a single hair."
The alms-bowl rice flows with fragrance; the stone image fulfills vows. "Stainless" is the inscription; the Master may indeed be seen.
The State Preceptor of the Song Dynasty, Dharma Master Ning (Ning Fashi).
His secular surname was Gao. His ancestors were people of Bohai. During the Tiānyòu era, the Master was born in Wú.
He was born at the Geese Villa in Deqing, Xingjun. He left home life at Xiangfu Monastery in Hangzhou and studied the Nanshan Vinaya school.
He composed treatises on the *vinaya*, for which his contemporaries called him the "Tiger of Vinaya. His literary talent flourished daily and his reputation grew increasingly eminent.
The princes and nobles of the Wu Su clan all admired and esteemed him, appointing him as the *Sengtong* (Patriarch) of the Two Zhe circuits and bestowing upon him the honorary title Mingyi Zongwen.

In the third year of the Xingguo era, Emperor Taizong heard of his reputation and issued an edict for him to appear before him at Zifu Hall. He was questioned there for many days and was subsequently granted the title Tonghui.

By imperial decree, he was commissioned to compile the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song* in thirty fascicles, and later ordered to compose the *Records of the Sages and Worthies of the Three Teachings* in one hundred fascicles.

Initially, he was appointed as the Head Lecturer of the Left Street and was charged with overseeing the affairs of the Buddhist teachings in the Western Capital. This was at the beginning of the Xianping era.

He was further appointed as the Monk Registrar (Senglù) of the Right Street. The Master also authored the *Neidian ji* (Collection of Inner Classics) in one hundred and fifty fascicles and the *Wai xue ji* (Collection of Outer Studies) in forty-nine fascicles.
Wang Yucheng, the Palace Secretary (Neihan), composed a preface for his collected works, praising them to the utmost.

He also wrote a letter commending his literary style, concluding with these words: "It is as if the seasonal rain has fallen and the sun and moon have emerged; the irrigation ditches and the torches are restored."
What was his purpose? He entered nirvana in the second year of the Zhizhi era and was buried in Longjingwu. In the fourth year of the Chongning era, he was posthumously granted the title Yuanming.

The eulogy says: His learning was vast and his realization was full; his fame resounded throughout the realm. Repeatedly wearing the plain silk headband, he repeatedly received imperial favor and was honored with official rank.
In the Translation Hall of the Imperial Historiography Bureau, the superfluous was excised and the essential was compiled; from antiquity to the present, its radiance is boundless.

There was the Dharma Master Suiyuan of the Song Dynasty, whose name was Jingyuan, his courtesy name Bichang, and his surname Yang. He was naturally gifted with keen intelligence from birth and relied upon Baoci Temple in the Eastern Capital.
Master Haida received ordination and resolved to seek out teachers for study. Initially, he met Chengqian of Huayan; next, he met Mingtan of Henghai;
and later, he met Zixuan of Changshui. He mastered the profound essentials of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and his reputation became widespread.
He resided at Qingliang in Quanzhou, Guanyin in Suzhou, Xiangfu in Hangzhou, Baoge in Huzhou, and Shanzhu in Xiuzhou. Left...
When Minister Pu Gong governed Hangzhou, he revered his Way and converted Huiyin Monastery from Chan to the Exoteric (Teaching) school, appointing the Master to reside there.

Wherever he went, both monastics and laypeople admired him with deep devotion. The Master’s calligraphy was powerful and vigorous; he combined the two commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* by Chengsheng and Zhengyuan into one for the convenience of study.
He also composed liturgical rites (*sān*) for the *Avataṃsaka*, *Śūraṅgama*, and *Awakening of Faith* sutras, as well as a ritual for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
He compiled the *Jiyi tongyao* (Essential Compendium of Collected Meanings) in fourteen fascicles. He also composed commentaries on sutras such as the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā*.

Prince Ui, known by his monastic name Tong Ikhyon, came from the Kingdom of Koryo by sea to inquire about the Dharma with the Master. The court dispatched the Court Lecturer Yang Jie to serve as his host;
that he could thus convert foreign lands makes the excellence of his Way evident. He passed away in the winter of the third year of the Yuanyou era.
He was cremated, and countless śarīras were obtained, which were interred to the northwest of Huìyīn Monastery. He was seventy-eight years of age.
In his previous life, he was a native of Jìnshuǐ in Quán; therefore, scholars referred to him as Jìnshuǐ. The eulogy says:
The Dharma-realm is inexhaustible; with a single mind, he penetrates its depths. Exerting his remaining strength, he expounded the various sutras to establish models and leave behind a standard.
Thus he acquired a magnificent reputation, and those who yearned for the Dharma were numerous; they set sail upon the ocean to reach his land.
